title: Password Management
subtopics: Why passwords must not be stored as plaintext

learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of password management in a FastAPI application.
Apply or interpret one example related to why passwords must not be stored as plaintext.
Identify one limitation or failure case and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson covers password management within authentication and authorization. Use the supplied syllabus topics as the coverage checklist, then connect them to the worked example and the verification task.
content.why_it_matters: You will use password management to build APIs whose contracts and behavior are understandable to both clients and maintainers. The practical aim is security boundaries, identity verification, least privilege and verifiable authorization decisions.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Password Management matters because it is part of authentication and authorization. In practice, focus on security boundaries, identity verification, least privilege and verifiable authorization decisions. A framework feature only helps when its assumptions match the application; keep input validation, business policy and side effects distinguishable.

items.title: Why passwords must not be stored as plaintext
items.text: Begin with the problem why passwords must not be stored as plaintext addresses. Describe the client, the data it sends, the decision the server makes, and the response that completes the contract. Keep framework responsibilities separate from business rules.

items.title: Password hashing
items.text: Treat password hashing as a trust-boundary concern. Verify identity and permissions on the server, use least privilege, keep secrets outside source control, and write negative tests for unauthorized access.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Password Management
content_blocks.expected_output: Without Authorization: Bearer <token>, the request is rejected. This demo does not authenticate or authorize the token.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Treat this as a security-scheme illustration only; never accept a token without cryptographic/issuer validation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For read-only examples, no reset is needed. For any example that writes state, use a disposable local database/test fixture; record the starting state and clean up only lab data. Never use production credentials or real personal data.
content_blocks.limitations: This code is inspectable lesson material, not executed by CodeLeaf. Run it only in a local virtual environment or a separately isolated runner with resource/time/network limits. Security examples are sketches, not complete production authentication or authorization systems.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Adapt the example to cover “Why passwords must not be stored as plaintext”. Write down the expected success result and one invalid, missing, duplicate, timeout or permission-boundary case that matters for this topic.

task: Create a small reviewable artifact for “Password Management”: explain its goal, cover the listed subtopics, show an example with expected result, then include one edge case and how you would verify it.
hints: Start with “Why passwords must not be stored as plaintext” and state the required inputs, output and assumptions.
Change one thing at a time; check the official reference and capture the actual response/error instead of guessing.
Include a negative/edge-case check and document which behavior remains untested.
expected_output: A reviewable example or design note for Password Management, covering the PDF subtopics, expected behavior and at least one verification check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a code fragment without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Installed versions, imported types, application structure and external services affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: State assumptions; check the versioned official docs; run a minimal local test and add one failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one happy-path response as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid input, permissions, concurrency, timeouts and cleanup are not exercised by a single request.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused normal and negative tests and record exact expected status/body.

common_mistakes.why: Even short examples may mutate records, reveal data or affect availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic inputs and a disposable environment; review security, cleanup and rollback before promotion.

summary: Password Management belongs to the broader goal of security boundaries, identity verification, least privilege and verifiable authorization decisions.
